title: What are Virtual Threads, what problem do they solve (cheap blocking for I/O-bound), when do they NOT help (CPU-bound), and what is thread pinning?

s1_definition.profdef: Virtual threads (Java 21, JEP 444) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM, not the OS. Millions can exist simultaneously (each ~1KB stack vs ~1MB for platform threads). They solve the C10K problem: traditional thread-per-request servers max out at ~5000-10000 threads due to OS limits and memory. Virtual threads make blocking I/O cheap — when a virtual thread blocks on I/O (DB query, HTTP call), the JVM unmounts it from its carrier (platform) thread and mounts another virtual thread. The carrier thread is NEVER idle. They do NOT help CPU-bound tasks — CPU work keeps the carrier occupied (no unmounting). Thread pinning occurs when a virtual thread cannot unmount (inside `synchronized` block or JNI call), blocking the carrier.
s1_definition.analogy: Platform threads = bank clerks (expensive, limited to 20 desks). Virtual threads = bank tokens (cheap, unlimited). Each token represents a customer waiting for a task. When one customer's task is waiting (I/O — like a background check), the clerk takes the next token. One clerk handles 1000 tokens by switching whenever someone waits. But if a customer needs the clerk's FULL ATTENTION (CPU-bound calculation), the clerk can't switch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Virtual thread = lightweight (~1KB), JVM-managed, unmounts on I/O block, millions possible. NOT for CPU-bound. Pinning = stuck on carrier inside synchronized/JNI. Use ReentrantLock for blocking in virtual threads.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Virtual threads (Java 21, JEP 444) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM, not the OS. Millions can exist simultaneously (each ~1KB stack vs ~1MB for platform threads). They solve the C10K problem: traditional thread-per-request servers max out at ~5000-10000 threads due to OS limits and memory. Virtual threads make blocking I/O cheap — when a virtual thread blocks on I/O (DB query, HTTP call), the JVM unmounts it from its carrier (platform) thread and mounts another virtual thread. The carrier thread is NEVER idle. They do NOT help CPU-bound tasks — CPU work keeps the carrier occupied (no unmounting). Thread pinning occurs when a virtual thread cannot unmount (inside `synchronized` block or JNI call), blocking the carrier.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Platform threads = bank clerks (expensive, limited to 20 desks). Virtual threads = bank tokens (cheap, unlimited). Each token represents a customer waiting for a task. When one customer's task is waiting (I/O — like a background check), the clerk takes the next token. One clerk handles 1000 tokens by switching whenever someone waits. But if a customer needs the clerk's FULL ATTENTION (CPU-bound calculation), the clerk can't switch.

**One line to remember:** Virtual thread = lightweight (~1KB), JVM-managed, unmounts on I/O block, millions possible. NOT for CPU-bound. Pinning = stuck on carrier inside synchronized/JNI. Use ReentrantLock for blocking in virtual threads.

sections.s2_technical:
Virtual threads (Project Loom, JEP 444, final in Java 21) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than the OS. Millions can exist at once because each costs a few hundred bytes, unlike platform threads which map 1:1 to costly OS threads. When a virtual thread BLOCKS on I/O (a database call, an HTTP request), the JVM unmounts it from its carrier platform thread and mounts another, so the OS thread is never idle.

You create them with `Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable)` or, more commonly, `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`, which spawns one virtual thread per task. The programming model stays simple and blocking — you write ordinary synchronous code (`conn.query(...)`) and the runtime handles the efficiency, avoiding the complexity of reactive/async callbacks.

A banking example: a service handling 50,000 concurrent transfer requests, each blocking on a database and a fraud-check HTTP call, can give each request its own virtual thread; the handful of carrier OS threads stay busy while thousands of virtual threads park on I/O. Senior nuance: virtual threads shine for I/O-bound, high-concurrency workloads; they do NOT speed up CPU-bound work, and you should not pool them — create one per task.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A transfer service using a fixed pool of 200 platform threads could not handle 50,000 concurrent requests that each blocked on a database and a fraud-check call; threads were exhausted and requests queued. Fix: virtual threads (one per request via `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor`) let thousands block on I/O cheaply while a few carrier threads stay busy.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: 10,000 tasks, each blocking briefly to simulate a DB/HTTP call.

**Step 2.** `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` creates one virtual thread per submitted task — cheap because each is a few hundred bytes.

**Step 3.** When a virtual thread sleeps (blocks), the JVM unmounts it from its carrier OS thread and mounts another, so OS threads never idle.

**Step 4.** `close()` on the try-with-resources executor waits for all 10,000 tasks to finish.

**Step 5.** All 10,000 tasks complete with only a handful of carrier threads.

```text
INFO: completed tasks = 10000 (thousands of virtual threads, few carriers)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ PLATFORM THREAD vs VIRTUAL THREAD ═══

  Platform Thread:                    Virtual Thread:
  ├─ OS-managed                       ├─ JVM-managed
  ├─ ~1MB stack                       ├─ ~1KB stack (grows as needed)
  ├─ Max ~5000-10000                  ├─ Millions possible
  ├─ Blocks carrier on I/O            ├─ UNMOUNTS on I/O → carrier freed!
  └─ $$$$ expensive to create         └─ ¢ cheap to create

  ═══ I/O-BOUND (virtual threads SHINE) ═══
  VT-1: HTTP call → unmounts → carrier handles VT-2
  VT-2: DB query → unmounts → carrier handles VT-3
  1 carrier serves 1000 virtual threads!

  ═══ CPU-BOUND (virtual threads DON'T HELP) ═══
  VT-1: Math.sin() loop → carrier BUSY → can't switch!
  → Use parallelStream/ForkJoinPool instead

  ═══ PINNING ═══
  synchronized(lock) { blockingIO(); }  → carrier STUCK (Java 21)
  ReentrantLock.lock() { blockingIO(); } → carrier FREE (unmounts)
  Java 24 (JEP 491): synchronized pinning REMOVED
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Virtual threads (Java 21) are lightweight JVM-managed threads that cost ~1KB each (vs ~1MB for platform threads). They enable millions of concurrent threads for I/O-bound workloads: when a virtual thread blocks on I/O (DB query, HTTP call, file read), the JVM unmounts it from its carrier thread and mounts another — the carrier is never idle. This solves the thread-per-request scalability limit. They do NOT help CPU-bound tasks because CPU work keeps the carrier occupied. Thread pinning occurs inside synchronized blocks (Java 21) where the virtual thread cannot unmount — fix by using ReentrantLock. Java 24 removes synchronized pinning. In Spring Boot: `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` makes all request threads virtual — instant scalability.
